title             : 'Exercise 3: Customising colour aesthetics'
output            : html_document
---


```{r setup, include = FALSE}
# No need to run this chunk unless you're "knitting"
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE,
                      comment= NA,
                      warning = FALSE,
                      message = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 6)
```

Load `tidyverse` package using the `library` function.

```{r}
# Load tidyverse
library(tidyverse)
```

Load our data.

```{r}
# Load the data
d_blomkvist <- read_csv("../../data/blomkvist.csv")

# Remove missing category for smoker and missing values for rt
d_blomkvist <- drop_na(d_blomkvist, smoker, rt_hand_d)
```

We will start with a plot that has enough ink to make changes visible. Add facets will allow you to see differences in the strips.


```{r}
# Make sure the strip text is informative
d_blomkvist <- mutate(d_blomkvist, meds_cat = str_c("medication: ", meds_cat))

plot_rt <- ggplot(d_blomkvist, aes(x = age, y = rt_hand_d, colour = smoker)) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~meds_cat) +
  labs(x = "Age in years", y = "Mean reaction time in msecs")

plot_rt
```
You can manually change the `theme` properties or use existing ones. For example, run the following code. We'll compare the plots using `patchwork`. Complete the missing bits in the code


```{r fig.width=10}
# Load package
library(patchwork)

# Create same plot with different themes
plot_bw <- --- + theme_bw() + labs(subtitle = "theme_bw")
plot_classic <- plot_rt + theme_classic() + labs(subtitle = "---")
plot_clean <- plot_rt + theme_---() + labs(subtitle = "theme_clean")
plot_light <- plot_rt + theme_light() + labs(subtitle = "theme_light")

# Combine all four plots
plot_bw + plot_classic + --- + plot_light

```
When you type `theme_` and you will see a drop-down list with all themes available in your environment. If you load `ggthemes` you will find even more themes to choose from. The name of the package a theme comes from is listed next to the drop-down list when you type `theme_` (after loading `ggthemes`).

```{r}
# Load package
library(ggthemes)

# Add a ggthemes theme
plot_rt + theme_---()
```
Lo and behold, there is even a `theme_tufte()`.


All themes allow you to change the base font size (default size varies). Choose a theme that you like and change the base size to 14

```{r}
plot_rt + theme_---(base_size = ---)
```


# ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
# Changing theme properties manually.
# Legend position: I prefer the legend to be on the top or bottom so there is
# more room for showing data when included on an A4 page.
# Also, I tend to remove the grid in the background when it doesn't serve a function.
rt_plot + theme(legend.position = "---", # use "top" or "bottom
                legend.justification = "right", # default is "centre". Use "right" or "left".
                panel.grid.minor = ---) # `element_blank()` can be use to remove properties such as minor grid lines

# Add the above changes to rt_plot using the assignment operator `<-` as above.



You can define themes from scratch but often it is easier to modify existing themes that already possess the properties you're interested in.








them modify themes


Creating your own theme

```{r}
theme_roeser <- theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.title = element_text(size = 14),
    panel.grid = element_blank(),
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.justification = "right"
  )
```

Setting your theme as default

```{r}
theme_set(theme_roeser)
```

All visualisations will now appear with your theme.

```{r}
ggplot(d_blomkvist, aes(x = age, y = rt_hand_d, colour = smoker)) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~meds_cat) +
  labs(x = "Age in years", y = "Mean reaction time in msecs")
```
